summary.headline: OAI-SearchBot (OpenAI's search/retrieval crawler) is granted unconditional 'Allow: /' -- more permissive than OpenAI's own ChatGPT-User, which is fully disallowed -- while PerplexityBot, a competing company's equivalent retrieval crawler, is also fully disallowed with no exceptions — critical severity, Confirm whether granting OAI-SearchBot unrestricted access while fully blocking ChatGPT-User and PerplexityBot reflects a deliberate, disclosed decision; if not, align their treatment.

findings.title: OAI-SearchBot (OpenAI's search/retrieval crawler) is granted unconditional 'Allow: /' -- more permissive than OpenAI's own ChatGPT-User, which is fully disallowed -- while PerplexityBot, a competing company's equivalent retrieval crawler, is also fully disallowed with no exceptions
findings.evidence: Verified directly against this project's robots.txt parser on multiple real content paths (/standings, /players, /team/lakers): OAI-SearchBot resolves 'allowed' unconditionally (a bare 'Allow: /' group with no restrictions at all). ChatGPT-User -- OpenAI's own agent for fetching a page in direct response to a live user request in ChatGPT -- resolves 'disallowed' on every path, with zero exceptions. PerplexityBot -- Perplexity's primary indexing/answer-engine crawler, the direct counterpart to OAI-SearchBot -- also resolves 'disallowed' on every path, with zero exceptions. Per this skill's own ai-crawler-agents.md, both OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot are retrieval-class agents whose blocking 'removes the brand from AI answers immediately' and 'is almost always unintentional' -- yet one is fully open and the other is fully closed, and even within OpenAI's own agent family, the search-indexing agent is treated more permissively than the live-user-request agent.

reproduction.observed: OAI-SearchBot: Allow: / (no restriction); ChatGPT-User: Disallow: / (no exception); PerplexityBot: Disallow: / (no exception)
reproduction.expected: Consistent treatment of equivalent retrieval-class agents across companies, and consistent treatment within a single company's own agent family, or a stated rationale for the difference

suggested_action.summary: Confirm whether granting OAI-SearchBot unrestricted access while fully blocking ChatGPT-User and PerplexityBot reflects a deliberate, disclosed decision; if not, align their treatment.
suggested_action.mechanism: As written, a fan asking ChatGPT or Perplexity for tonight's standings or a player's stats can be served an NBA.com-sourced answer only through OAI-SearchBot's indexing path, never through a live ChatGPT-User fetch or through Perplexity at all -- an asymmetry in AI-answer-engine visibility that is easy to miss when only checking robots.txt for a single yes/no verdict on 'AI crawlers.'
steps: Confirm with the team that maintains this file whether the OAI-SearchBot/ChatGPT-User/PerplexityBot split is intentional.
If not intentional, extend OAI-SearchBot's treatment (or the GPTBot group's Allow exceptions) to ChatGPT-User and PerplexityBot consistently.
suggested_action.verification: OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User and PerplexityBot receive the same treatment, or the file states why one is treated differently.

findings.title: robots.txt declares the 'GPTBot' and 'Google-Extended' user-agent groups twice each, with materially different and conflicting rules -- a genuinely malformed file whose effective policy for these two agents depends entirely on which parser implementation a given crawler happens to use
findings.evidence: The file contains 'User-agent: GPTBot' twice: the first occurrence pairs 'Disallow: /' with nine specific Allow exceptions covering most core content (standings, schedule, stats pages, player profiles, team pages); the second occurrence, appearing later in the same file, pairs 'Disallow: /' with zero exceptions. 'User-agent: Google-Extended' is duplicated identically. This project's own parser, verified directly, resolves the duplication by merging both groups' rules into one combined ruleset (allowing /standings, /players, /team/lakers while disallowing an unlisted path) -- a defensible interpretation, but not the only one a real crawler could reach. The robots.txt specification does not define behavior for repeated groups naming the same agent, and real-world parsers disagree: some honor only the first group encountered for a given agent (Google's own documented behavior), others only the last, others merge as this project's parser does. A GPTBot-respecting crawler using a stricter, last-group-wins parser would see nothing but a blanket 'Disallow: /' with no exceptions at all for the exact same file this audit read as granting access to standings, schedules and player pages.

reproduction.observed: 2 (and 2 for Google-Extended), with different Allow/Disallow rules attached to each occurrence
reproduction.expected: Exactly one group per named agent, so every compliant parser reaches the same, unambiguous verdict

suggested_action.summary: Consolidate the two GPTBot groups (and the two Google-Extended groups) into a single group each, stating the intended rule set once.
suggested_action.mechanism: This is very likely an artifact of the file being edited by more than one process or team over time without either noticing the other's existing group for the same agent, rather than a deliberate policy -- and because different real crawlers parse duplicate groups differently, the site cannot currently know with confidence what its own robots.txt actually communicates to GPTBot or Gemini's training crawler.
steps: Locate both 'User-agent: GPTBot' blocks and merge them into one, deciding definitively whether the Allow exceptions are intended to apply.
Repeat for the two 'User-agent: Google-Extended' blocks.
Add a lint check to whatever process generates or edits this file to catch duplicate User-agent declarations before publishing.
suggested_action.verification: Each named agent appears in exactly one User-agent group in the file.

not_assessed.check: Structured data on individual player, team, and game pages beyond the homepage; answerability; freshness/corroboration; engagement
not_assessed.reason: This run hand-verified the robots.txt file in depth (finding both the duplicate-group defect and the retrieval-agent asymmetry) rather than sampling content pages broadly. The homepage itself carries real, well-formed SportsOrganization, WebPage and BreadcrumbList JSON-LD, a positive signal this run did not extend further.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot say whether the same structured-data quality holds on player, team or live-game pages, or whether game/event pages carry SportsEvent markup with correct dates and scores -- a genuine gap in this run, not a claim either way about the site.

not_assessed.reason: No headless-browser engine (Playwright/Puppeteer) was available in this run's environment.
not_assessed.impact: Cannot assess the actual on-site experience for a JavaScript-executing visitor.
